templates.text: {first} says {second} moved the boundary stone a furrow's width. {second} says it was always there.

options.label: Hire a surveyor and split the difference
Rule for {first} and cover the surveyor's fee
Rule for {second} and waive the field's tithe

templates.expired: The surveyor came, measured twice and charged for both. {first} and {second} agree only that it cost too much.

templates.text: {first} lent {second} a plough in spring. It came back with one handle.

options.label: Pay for a new handle
Make {second} pay {first} for it
Call it fair wear

templates.expired: The handle was replaced at the steward's expense, and {first} and {second} are no friendlier for it.

templates.text: {first} accuses {second} of stealing a hen. {second} has a hen, and a great deal to say about it.

options.label: Buy {first} a new hen
Fine {second} for the steward's trouble
Dismiss the charge

templates.expired: A hen was bought, and both {first} and {second} are certain it was the wrong one.

templates.text: {first} promised a dowry to {second}'s family and now disputes the count of the sheaves.

options.label: Make up the shortfall from the stores
Hold {first} to the full count
Tell {second} to accept less, with a gift to ease the sting

templates.expired: The stores covered the shortfall. {first} and {second} now disagree about who owes the steward thanks.

templates.text: {first} and {second} both claim the first grinding of the day at the mill.

options.label: Draw up a rota and a fee
Give {first} the mornings, fee waived
Give {second} the mornings and a sack of flour on the house

templates.expired: A rota went up on the mill door. {first} and {second} have each already found a fault in it.

templates.text: {second}'s pigs have eaten through {first}'s fence and, by report, most of {first}'s cabbages.

options.label: Pay to mend the fence
Order {second} to pay {first}, less a fee for the paperwork
Say pigs will be pigs

templates.expired: The fence was mended. {second}'s pigs have already noted the weak point.

templates.text: {first} says {second} draws water with a bucket twice the usual size, and that the well has noticed.

options.label: Fix a bucket size and pay for the new rope
Rule for {first} and have the bucket cut down
Rule that water is water

templates.expired: A bucket size was fixed by decree. {second} found that two smaller buckets hold exactly as much, and {first} has taken it personally.

templates.text: {first} says {second} gleaned the field before the reapers had finished. {second} says the reapers were slow.

options.label: Hand {first} a sheaf from the stores to settle it
Order {second} to return the gleanings, with a fine on top
Rule that grain on the ground belongs to the quick

templates.expired: A sheaf changed hands from the stores. {first} thinks it was too small and {second} thinks it was too late.

templates.text: {first} owes {second} a long tab at the alehouse and has offered an opinion of the ale in place of coin.

options.label: Pay the tab from the treasury and call it civic hospitality
Tell {second} that an opinion is worth something
Make {first} work off the tab, and take a small fee for the trouble

templates.expired: The treasury paid the tab. The alehouse has since named a stew after the steward.

templates.text: {first} and {second} both say the woodpile between their houses is theirs, and each has been burning it.

options.label: Buy what is left for the village
Give the pile to {first} and take a tithe of it
Give the pile to {second} and say nothing of the tithe

templates.expired: The village bought the remains of the woodpile. It was mostly ash, and nobody will say who held the match.

templates.text: {first} calls {second}'s rooster a menace. {second} calls it a clock.

options.label: Pay {first} to stop complaining
Order the rooster penned, at {second}'s cost
Rule that dawn is not an offence

templates.expired: {first} was paid to stop complaining. The rooster, unpaid, did not.

templates.text: A travelling smith offers two coin an ore, which is twice the market price, and would like it before he thinks better of it.

options.label: Sell him ten ore
Sell him four ore
Send him on

templates.expired: The smith waited for a steward, then for a reason to stay, and took his money to the next village.

templates.text: A timber factor wants wood for a bridge that someone else will be asked to pay for. He offers nine-tenths of a coin each.

options.label: Sell thirty wood
Sell ten wood
Decline the contract

templates.expired: The factor left unpaid and unbothered, muttering about rural procurement.

templates.text: A grain factor with a full cart and a short temper will sell below the market price, if you take it today.

options.label: Buy the whole cart: forty grain
Buy half a cart: twenty grain
Let the cart go

templates.expired: The cart rolled on. Somewhere down the road, a steward is being very pleasant to a grain factor.

templates.text: A cooper with a barrel order and no oak will pay a full coin for each piece of wood, and would rather not discuss the barrels.

options.label: Sell him fifteen wood
Sell him five wood
Tell him to cut his own oak

templates.expired: The cooper looked at the forest, then at the steward, and went to look at someone else's forest.

templates.text: A baker from the market town needs grain for a wedding and has more coin than patience.

options.label: Sell him thirty grain
Sell him fifteen grain
Say the stores are not for weddings

templates.expired: The baker found grain elsewhere. The wedding went ahead and the bread was reported to be adequate.

templates.text: A pedlar has a sack of ore that he swears fell off nothing in particular, and will part with it cheaply.

options.label: Buy the sack: twelve ore
Buy half the sack: six ore
Ask where it fell from

templates.expired: The pedlar shouldered his sack and left, muttering about stewards and their suspicions.

templates.text: A charcoal burner has run out of cordwood and will trade ore for it, without explaining what he intends to do with so much wood.

options.label: Swap twenty wood for eight ore
Swap ten wood for four ore
Keep the wood

templates.expired: The charcoal burner left, black to the elbows and unbothered.

templates.text: A stranger with a bedroll and no references asks to settle, along with whoever is trailing behind. She says they are all good with their hands, and has not said which hands.

options.label: Let them settle, and feed them first
Send them on their way

templates.expired: The stranger's party walked on, still unreferenced, still good with their hands.

templates.text: A cartwright says the last village was full, loudly and with some bitterness. He and anyone travelling with him will farm for their keep if the first meal is on you.

options.label: Admit them and cover the first meal
Wish them luck at the next village

templates.expired: The cartwright shouldered his tools, gathered whoever had come with him, and went to find a village that was not full.

templates.text: A pilgrim on her way to a shrine two provinces off asks for beds for herself and any fellow pilgrims. She has been on her way for six years.

options.label: Give them beds and a first meal
Point them toward the shrine

templates.expired: The pilgrim thanked the village on behalf of all present and continued toward a shrine she would likely never reach.

templates.text: A tinker's wagon has lost a wheel and the tinker has lost the will to mend it. He, and whoever rides with him, would sooner mend your tools than their own.

options.label: Take them on and feed them while they work
Lend them a wheel and send them on

templates.expired: The tinker patched the wagon with optimism and left. The wheel was seen on the road a mile on.

templates.text: A widow with a handcart, a good deal of opinion and no remaining family asks if the village has a corner for her and any stragglers she has collected on the road.

options.label: Make room and cover their first meals
Say the village has no corner to spare

templates.expired: The widow looked at the village, then at the steward, and made it clear which had disappointed her more.

templates.text: {name} arrives with a letter of recommendation from a lord you have never met. They offer to run {village} peasants at {job}, and are known to be {traits}. The fee is {price} coin.

options.label: Take on {name}
Thank {name} and send them home

templates.expired: {name} tucked the letter away and went to offer the same village to someone else.

templates.text: {name}, late of a quieter province, would govern {village} peasants at {job}. Those who have worked with them call them {traits}. They want {price} coin to begin.

options.label: Engage {name}
Decline politely

templates.expired: {name} waited as long as courtesy asked, then took the road back.

templates.text: A petitioner named {name} says {village} peasants are waiting for a governor and will work {job} under one. Their references describe them as {traits}. The price is {price} coin.

options.label: Appoint {name}
Tell {name} the posts are filled

templates.expired: {name} left the petition on the desk and was not seen again.

templates.text: Two auditors from the crown have arrived with their own ledger and a great deal of patience. They would like the stores to match the books.

options.label: Open the stores and cover the books in full
Pay them to find the books in order, and keep the difference on paper

templates.expired: The auditors counted what was there, wrote down what was not, and left with the first and a note about the second.

templates.text: A royal examiner has sealed the granary door and asks, courteously, to see what the books say is behind it.

options.label: Break the seal and make the stores match the books
Pay the examiner's fee and hope he stops counting

templates.expired: The examiner broke the seal himself, took what was behind it, and was not pleased by the rest.

templates.text: {first} asks leave to send for a cousin, who is said to be hardworking and, at worst, hungry.

options.label: Send for the cousin and feed the journey
Send a sack of grain for the cousin's trouble
Tell {first} the village is full enough

templates.expired: A sack of grain went to the cousin, who has since decided that the journey was not necessary.

templates.text: {first}'s roof has opened to the weather, and {first} asks for wood and the loan of a hand to put it right.

options.label: Send the wood and a hand, to be repaid in labor
Send a few bundles of thatch and your sympathy
Tell {first} that rain is good for the crops

templates.expired: A few bundles of thatch arrived. {first} has made a bucket of the largest hole.

templates.text: {first} asks for coin to buy better seed, and promises to repay it at harvest with something over.

options.label: Lend the coin and wait for the harvest
Lend a few coins, to be paid back in due course
Tell {first} that seed is seed

templates.expired: A few coins went out. {first} bought what seed it could and has not been seen near the treasury since.

templates.text: {first} asks for grain for a name-day feast, and says the whole village will remember who made it possible.

options.label: Fund the feast and let the village remember
Send a sack and a good wish
Tell {first} that memory is not a harvest

templates.expired: A sack and a good wish went out. The feast was small, and {first} will say so for some time.

templates.text: A traveller who reads the shoulder-bones of sheep predicts a lean season, and would like to be thanked in advance.

options.label: Pay for a granary roof against the damp
Buy in an extra sack before prices rise
Thank him and ignore him

templates.expired: The traveller left, offended, with his sheep. No one in the village mentions what the winter was like.

templates.text: A drover says the geese flew south a month early and that, in his experience, geese are never wrong about winter.

options.label: Patch the granary roof and stack the grain higher
Say geese are cheap and so is advice

templates.expired: The drover drove on. The geese, wherever they were, were seen to be right.

templates.text: A wandering friar reads the moss on the north walls and says the coming year will be a hungry one, and that he is sorry about it.

options.label: Mend the granary roof and seal the bins
Tell him to save his moss for the abbey

templates.expired: The friar blessed the village and left it to the moss.
